newsitem.title: USA: First ever options trading in antimony launched.
newsitem.headline: First ever options trading in antimony launched.

text.p: New York trading company Oxxides Inc has set up what it claims is the first options market for antimony, although other dealers remain skeptical.
"We have had inquiries about it, but we have not gotten anybody that's anxious to jump into it just yet," said Oxxides vice president John Allick.
Antimony, a metal whose production is dominated by China, is used mainly in fire retardants. It is usually sold on spot or long-term contracts, often linked to published third-party prices.
"This is a new way of doing business, but nobody has bought any options yet," Allick said.
Options give the holder the right to buy from, or sell to, Oxxides at any time before the expiration date a specified quantity of antimony at an agreed price.
The Oxxides options are not registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

In a statement to customers issued in late September, Oxxides quoted a January 1997 strike price of $1.25 per lb, with the cost of a call option at three cents a lb, or the income per lb for put option at one cent.
Antimony prices were quoted last week at $0.95 to $1.02 per lb in warehouse Rotterdam.
Oxxides said the options contracts cover a minimum of 20-ton lots of Chinese high tint antimony trioxide Twinkling Star brand.
John Gustavsen of Antimony Products of America, a producer of antimony and fire retardants, said Oxxides' options were not being taken seriously yet.
"I don't see anybody get rich on this. Antimony is as easy to buy as beach sand, so why in the world would you want to complicate it," Gustavsen said.
Several traders said the antimony was plentiful and there would be a lack of speculators to inject liquidity and take on risk in the market.
Consumers would probably be the key users of options. "The consumers I have talked to are beffudled," one dealer said.
